title: The Great Trap
reviewNotes: Significant source correction: complete initial seven-piece diagram is drawn; Rb8 remains drawn because ...Ra4 (and other fourth-rank moves) holds. The source’s ...Rb2+ loses, and only then is Ke1 a winning retreat. Practice begins after that error at 74 seconds. Four branches check the mating line, two drawing exchanges and representative independent Black drawing defense; all steps saved.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players [music] might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible [music] win that white has in this position. It might seem like black is completely winning, having an extra pawn that is only one square away from [music] getting a new queen, but it is not that simple. It is white to move, and white has a bishop that can check the king. Unfortunately though, if we do give a check, the rook is just going to sacrifice itself, and from this position, after king to B2, white is going to have to give the rook for the queen, and this [music] would be a draw. So, from that starting position, white has to come up with a more original idea. And indeed, white plays rook to B8. A mysterious move. Of course, this sacrifices the rook right away, but interestingly enough, this rook cannot be taken, because if black does take the rook, now after bishop to D4 check, the rook has to come down to B2, but after king to C1, the king and the bishop work together to deliver a checkmate. But black is not naive enough to allow that. And so, instead of taking the seemingly free rook, he plays rook to B2 check, trying to give [music] up the rook on his own terms. Now, if white takes, after king takes, again, black is threatening the promotion, and we are only left with a bishop, and this would be a draw. So, is this it? Is black simply out of the woods? Well, not exactly. White has the brilliant and majestic and seemingly counterintuitive >> [music] >> king E1. A beautiful move that steps away from the action, but paradoxically, is the only winning move in this position. And all of a sudden, black realizes that he's completely lost. First of all, if the rook moves away, this would just be a checkmate in two moves. And if instead of that, the bishop tries to move, we're going to pin the rook to the king when it on the next move and stop the promotion of the pawn, and this would be an easy win. But this is not over quite yet, because of course, after king to e1, black still has the option of capturing the rook. And now the king is too far away to deliver the checkmate, or at least you would think that. But after bishop to d4 check, the only move is rook to b2. And now king to d1 doesn't change anything. On the next move, the king is going to come to c1, no matter what. The king, the rook, and the pawn are all paralyzed in their position, and this light-squared bishop cannot interact in any way with the dark-squared bishop. So no matter where the bishop moves, king c1 is going to follow. And on the next move, bishop to b2 is going to be a majestic checkmate.
